headline: 75.9°F at the Bight Buoy — the Filament Finally Kissed the Canyon Wall
subhead: A three-degree jump on the shelf pushed warm water onto the edge, and the yellowfin followed it right to the Dip.
body_markdown:
Buoy 44025 out in the Bight is reading 75.9°F this morning, running a solid three-plus degrees warmer than what we were seeing two weeks back. That number matters more than it looks. Shelf water in the high 70s means the filament that's been teasing us off the canyon edge finally pushed inshore enough to override the cooler upwelling that had the yellowfin scattered and deep. Wave state is nothing to write home about — 3.6 feet at a 6-second period, mean direction out of the south — a little sloppy on the ride out but nothing that shuts down a spread once you're on the grounds.

I ran 68 nautical miles out of Manasquan Tuesday to the Dip, roughly the 39°32'N, 72°32'W stretch, and the water column told the story before we even wet a line. Color went from a dirty green shelf water to a clean cobalt blue right at the 100-fathom curl, and the temp gauge on the troll spread jumped almost two degrees in under a mile. That's the kind of kink we flagged last week — said if the SST break sharpened or bent over the canyon's east elbow, that corner would be the spot — and that's exactly where we found bait balled up and birds working tight circles.

Yellowfin were on the warm side of that break, mostly 20 to 40 pounds, with a couple pushing 50. We picked them up trolling a mixed spread — green machines and small ballyhoo skirted in blue/white on the short riggers, a spreader bar with squid chains down the center, cedar plugs way back. The fish wanted the smaller offerings once the sun got up high; naked ballyhoo behind a small green/yellow bird outfished the bigger bar two to one by midday. Bigeye showed up on the overnight drift — we chunked butterfish over the edge between the Claw and the Dip starting around 9 p.m., dropped glow-stick rigged baits to 150 feet, and connected on two bigeye in the 80-100 pound class before 2 a.m. That bite dies fast once the current lays down, so timing the drift to the building tide matters more than people give it credit for.

Mahi were scattered but not absent — found a decent weed line drifting northeast off the temp break holding gaffer-sized fish, 8 to 15 pounds, plus a pile of schoolies that came up on chunks the second we slowed the boat. If you find floating structure — a pallet, a bucket, anything — stop and pitch a bucktail or a small ballyhoo before you troll past it. Wahoo have been an incidental catch on the high-speed gear, one solid 45-pounder taken on a black/purple Braid Marauder run at 14 knots along the break, but nobody's targeting them specifically yet — the water hasn't held long enough at that clean blue color to build a real pattern.

White marlin are around but thin. We raised two off the Claw on the troll — both came unbuttoned before the pitch bait connected — and heard of one release out near Texas Tower on the way home. Not enough volume yet to call it a pattern, more a bonus if you're already tuna trolling and keep dredge teasers in the water.

Bluefin haven't materialized at the canyon itself this stretch — that fish is showing further north and east right now, more a Block Island and Stellwagen story as warm water pushes bait that direction. If bluefin are the target, I'd look elsewhere this week rather than burn fuel hunting them at Hudson.

Swordfish scouting during the day has been quiet but not dead — we marked bait stacked tight to bottom in 1,400 feet off the southwest edge of the canyon on the sounder, the kind of structure that usually holds a daytime drift. Haven't had the right window to put a squid-and-light rig down there yet, but that's on the list for next trip if the sea state cooperates.

Tides are softening out of the recent push, easing toward the next neap phase, and that's exactly the setup where trolling starts gaining share over the chunk — less current means baits track cleaner and fish have an easier time committing to a moving target instead of holding tight to a chunk slick. We called that shift last week and it's playing out — troll numbers this week beat the chunk numbers for the first time in a month.

Looking ahead, if that filament holds its position and the break stays sharp over the east elbow, I'd run the same coordinates again before I'd chase anything new — the Dip through the Claw, working the blue-water side of the 100-fathom line. If a front pushes through and knocks that warm tongue back offshore, the bite likely follows it out past the canyon proper, and you'd be running an extra 15-20 miles to find the same water. Watch the color change on the way out before you commit to a spot — it's telling you more right now than any single number on a gauge.
